analysis.one_liner: Lets states opt out of major Affordable Care Act rules covering insurance and Medicaid.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a Health subcommittee, and died when the 113th Congress ended without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any state pass a law to exempt itself from major parts of the Affordable Care Act, including rules on what insurance must cover, requirements that people and employers carry coverage, the health insurance exchanges, and the expansion of Medicaid. A state could keep its pre-2010 health insurance rules, and could return to the ACA later by repealing its opt-out law. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, states would gain the choice to run health insurance under their own rules instead of the ACA's. Healthier, younger residents of a state that opted out could see lower premiums, since insurers could sell plans that skip the ACA's benefit requirements. Insurers in such a state would gain freedom to sell skimpier, cheaper plans without the guaranteed-coverage and benefit mandates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: States opting out; insurers; healthier buyers

how_it_helps.text: Would let a state, by passing its own law, pick which ACA provisions apply to it — including essential health benefits rules, the individual and employer coverage mandates, the exchanges, and the Medicaid expansion [S2][S3].
Would let a state revert to its health coverage laws as they stood on March 23, 2010, or to later state laws, and would let it return to the ACA by repealing the opt-out law [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: In a state that opts out, residents with pre-existing conditions would lose the ACA guarantee that insurers must cover them and charge them standard rates, and people needing comprehensive coverage would face higher premiums as healthier buyers shift to skimpier plans. Low-income adults in such a state would forgo the Medicaid expansion path to coverage, and hospitals there would lose the Medicaid expansion payments that offset uncompensated care.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick residents, low-income adults, hospitals in opt-out states

drawbacks.text: A state that opted out could drop the ACA's essential health benefits and its guaranteed-issue rules, which means insurers could deny coverage or charge sharply higher prices to people with pre-existing conditions [S2][S3].
An opt-out state could turn down the ACA's Medicaid expansion, closing off the coverage route the law created for low-income adults [S2].
Losing the ACA's framework could raise premiums for people who need comprehensive coverage, as healthier buyers move to cheaper, less complete plans [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives states real flexibility, but its cost falls on the people least able to bear it: in any opt-out state, the protections that matter most to people with medical conditions and the Medicaid expansion for low-income adults would be on the chopping block alongside the rules critics call burdensome. Whether that trade is worth it would depend entirely on each state's choices, and the bill sets no floor of protections states must keep.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, sent to a Health subcommittee, and never moved further before the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mick Mulvaney, joined by Rep. Trey Gowdy, introduced the bill on November 21, 2013 [S1][S3].
The House referred it to two committees — Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means — the same day [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
It had only two cosponsors, both Republicans, and died at the end of the 113th Congress without a hearing or vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the ACA's benefit mandates, guaranteed-coverage rules, and Medicaid expansion remained in place nationwide; state flexibility advocates and insurers seeking lighter regulation gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Trey Gowdy
for.what_they_did: Joined Mulvaney in introducing the bill.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; both Republicans.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat at the Health subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the provisions within its jurisdiction.

sides.party_line_note: Every named supporter was a Republican; the bill drew no Democratic cosponsors and never came to a vote.

industries.note: In a state that opted out, insurers could sell plans free of the ACA's benefit and coverage mandates, but would also lose the ACA's subsidized-customer structure in that state. Their lighter-regulation gain would come partly at the cost of sick customers who rely on guaranteed coverage [S2][S3].

A state that opted out of the Medicaid expansion would forgo federal expansion payments, leaving hospitals to absorb more uncompensated care while low-income residents went without the new coverage route [S2].
